passage: Clara's water bottle was on the kitchen bench again, the third time that week. At school in Wellington, her spelling sheet had vanished somewhere between her desk and the bus. Yet on Sunday she had spent four straight hours building a cardboard model of a volcano, labels and all. When her dad, Noa, found the bottle, Clara's shoulders went up to her ears. "I know, I know. I'm hopeless." Noa sat down beside her. "You're not hopeless. The volcano took you four hours." Together they drew pictures on a card by the door: bottle, lunchbox, folder, hat. The next morning Clara tapped each picture before she left, and the bottle went with her.

qa.q: What did Clara build on Sunday?
qa.a: She built a cardboard model of a volcano, labels and all.

qa.q: How was Clara feeling when her dad found the bottle, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt bad and ashamed; her shoulders went up to her ears and she called herself hopeless.

qa.q: What choice did Noa make instead of scolding Clara?
qa.a: He reminded her of the four-hour volcano and drew a picture card with her by the door, which worked the very next morning.

qa.q: How does Noa see Clara's forgetting?
qa.a: He sees it as a routine problem, not laziness, because he knows she can focus for hours when something interests her.

grounding: A child forgets and loses things but works for hours when interested, feels bad at reminders, and a picture checklist helps more than scolding.

passage: By Wednesday, Uma's desk in Class 6B held a pile of loose paper, a nest of pencil shavings and no maths worksheet. The class monitor sighed loudly. "Again, Uma?" Uma stared at her knees. In the afternoon, though, when the class began the plant experiment, she was the one who stayed through break measuring seedlings and drawing every leaf. Their teacher, Francis, noticed both. After school Francis taped a small card to her desk with three drawings: a red folder, a pencil, a tick. "Everything with a tick goes in the red folder before the bell. That's all." On Friday the worksheet came back, crumpled but complete. Uma grinned and tapped the card.

qa.q: What did Uma do during break in the plant experiment?
qa.a: She stayed through break measuring seedlings and drawing every leaf.

qa.q: What does Uma staring at her knees suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels embarrassed and bad about being reminded again in front of the class.

qa.q: What choice did Francis make after noticing both sides of Uma?
qa.a: Francis gave her a simple picture card and one rule about the red folder instead of a telling-off, and the worksheet came back.

qa.q: How might the monitor see Uma after watching her in the plant experiment?
qa.a: The monitor might realise she is not lazy, since she worked right through break when something caught her interest.

grounding: A schoolgirl loses worksheets but throws herself into what interests her, and a teacher's simple visual card helps more than scolding.

passage: The school bus horn sounded at the corner, and Rehana still had one shoe on. 'Worksheet?' Ammi called. Rehana froze. She had spent last evening building a water-cycle model from a plastic bottle and cotton wool, so absorbed she had forgotten dinner, and the signed worksheet was somewhere. So was her water bottle. 'Every day, Rehana! Every single day!' Ammi's voice rose. Rehana's eyes stung. She wasn't trying to forget. Her older sister Zainab dug the worksheet out from under the model, squashed but whole, and pushed it into the bag. That evening Zainab taped a card to the door with five drawings: bottle, tiffin, worksheet, pencil box, shoes. 'Touch each one before you go,' she said. 'Like a game.'

qa.q: What did Rehana build the evening before?
qa.a: A water-cycle model from a plastic bottle and cotton wool.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when Ammi shouted 'Every day'?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, her eyes stinging, because she wasn't forgetting on purpose.

qa.q: Why might Zainab's card work better than scolding?
qa.a: It turns remembering into a simple picture routine Rehana can touch each morning, instead of leaving her feeling bad.

qa.q: What is the rushed morning like for Ammi?
qa.a: Ammi is stressed and frustrated, with the bus waiting and the same things missing again, which is why her voice rose.

grounding: Shows a child who loses worksheets and bottles while absorbed in bursts of interest, feels bad when scolded, and is helped by a visual checklist.

passage: Lavanya had ignored the science project for three weeks. Then on Thursday night, after reading about bees, she built a cardboard hive with forty hexagons and stayed up till eleven. On Friday, Rafiq Sir held it up for the class. Then he asked for the maths worksheet. Lavanya went through her bag twice: a bee drawing, an old bus pass, a hair clip. No worksheet. Her face burned. 'Sorry, Sir. Again.' Two boys snickered. At break Rafiq Sir called her over and handed her a clear yellow folder with two labels: HOMEWORK IN, HOMEWORK OUT. 'Everything goes here, nowhere else. Show me on Monday.' Lavanya held it with both hands, the colour of her hive.

qa.q: What did Lavanya build on Thursday night?
qa.a: A cardboard hive with forty hexagons.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's face burning suggest?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed at forgetting the worksheet again, especially with two boys snickering.

qa.q: What made Rafiq Sir's folder a better response than a scolding?
qa.a: It gave her one clear place for homework and a small check on Monday, a routine that helps rather than shames.

qa.q: How might Rafiq Sir see Lavanya after the hive?
qa.a: He likely sees a capable, eager child who works in bursts, not a lazy one, which is why he offered help instead of punishment.

grounding: Shows a child who works in bursts of interest and keeps losing worksheets, and a teacher who offers a simple routine instead of a scolding.

passage:
'Ira Didi, don't tell Papa.'
'Tell him what?'
'The bottle. The blue one. It's gone.'
'That's the third one this term, Hemant.'
'I know!' His voice cracked. 'I put it down to catch a grasshopper at recess, then the bell went. I'm not lazy. I don't do it on purpose.'
'I know you're not lazy. You drew that whole grasshopper in ten minutes. Your brain just runs after the interesting thing.'
'So what do I do?'
Ira held up a metal clip from her drawer. 'This goes on the bottle. The bottle clips to your bag. It never comes off, even for grasshoppers.'
'Even really big ones?'
'Especially those.'
Hemant almost smiled. 'Will you tell Papa?'
'We'll tell him together. And show him the clip.'

qa.q: Why did Hemant put the bottle down at recess?
qa.a: To catch a grasshopper.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when his voice cracked?
qa.a: He felt upset and ashamed, worried about being called lazy when he never forgets on purpose.

qa.q: What did Ira get right in helping Hemant?
qa.a: She believed he wasn't lazy and gave him a simple fix, a clip that keeps the bottle on his bag, instead of a lecture.

qa.q: Why might Ira say 'We'll tell him together'?
qa.a: Ira seems to guess Hemant is scared of Papa's reaction, and wants to stand beside him while showing the plan.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps losing bottles when interest pulls him away, feels bad about it, and is helped by a simple routine rather than scolding.

passage: When I was ten, I lost something almost every day. I'm Shankar. My water bottle, my library book, the permission slip for the zoo trip. Amma would sigh, "Again?" and I'd feel hot and ashamed, like I was bad. But I wasn't lazy. Some nights I'd get an idea and build a whole volcano model till midnight, totally focused. Then I'd forget where I put my shoes. One Sunday Amma stopped scolding. She stuck a picture checklist on the door: bottle, bag, book, tiffin, with little drawings. Every morning I touched each picture before leaving. I still forgot sometimes, but much less. And Amma said "Good job" more than "Again?"

qa.q: What did Amma stick on the door?
qa.a: A picture checklist: bottle, bag, book, tiffin, with little drawings.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when Amma said "Again?"
qa.a: Shankar felt hot and ashamed, as if being forgetful meant being bad.

qa.q: Why did the checklist work better than scolding?
qa.a: It gave a simple visual routine to follow each morning, so Shankar forgot less and heard more praise than reminders.

qa.q: How might Amma feel saying "Good job" more often?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and happier, glad the checklist replaced daily frustration.

grounding: Shows a child who forgets things and works in bursts when interested, feels bad about reminders, and is helped by a visual checklist rather than scolding.
